1:
Gill treats the opening verb as a modest expression, and reports the rabbinic view of Jarchi and others that it means Adam had known his wife before he sinned, since otherwise he would not have observed the command to be fruitful; but if children had been begotten in innocence they would have been free from the corruption of nature afterwards contracted, so he prefers the opinion that some considerable time passed, one chronicler putting it at thirty years after the expulsion from paradise. Calvin makes the same point doctrinally rather than chronologically: the benediction to increase and multiply was not abolished by sin, and the heart of Adam was divinely confirmed so that he did not shrink with horror from the production of offspring; yet as he recognised at the very commencement of having offspring the truly paternal moderation of God's anger, so he was afterwards compelled to taste the bitter fruits of his own sin when Cain slew Abel. Both Calvin and Henry think the brothers were twins, Calvin because Moses commemorates a double birth while speaking of only one conception, and Henry because the pair recall Esau and Jacob, the elder hated and the younger loved.

What Eve meant by her exclamation is the chief question. Clarke calls it extremely difficult to ascertain, and rejects the common view that she took Cain for the promised seed as too refined for that period; more likely she meant no more than to acknowledge that it was through God's peculiar blessing that she conceived, and that she now had a well-grounded hope the race of man would continue. Unless she had been under divine inspiration, he adds, she could not have called her son Jehovah, and that she was not so inspired her mistake sufficiently proves. Calvin lists three renderings, with the Lord, from the Lord, and through the Lord, which all tend to the same point, that Eve gives thanks for a posterity she had deserved never to have; he rejects the subtler reading which makes her claim the promised conqueror already in her arms, and takes her rather to be offering the child to God as the first-fruits of his race, calling a newborn infant a man because she saw the human race renewed which she and her husband had ruined. Ellicott alone presses the harder rendering, who is Jehovah, on the ground that the particle cannot mean one thing here and another in the first verse of the book; the objection that this implies too advanced a knowledge he calls unfounded, since we read backward and put our own ideas into the narrative, whereas these words were only the germ, the filament in the acorn which contains the oak. In Eve's mouth the title probably meant no more than the coming One.

The names are read for their sense. Henry and Wesley take Cain for possession, spoken with joy and thankfulness and great expectation, and Henry adds the warning: if she did think this son the promised seed she was wretchedly mistaken, as Samuel was when he said, Surely the Lord's anointed is before me. When children are born, who can foresee what they will prove? He that was thought to be a man from the Lord became an enemy to the Lord, and the less we expect from creatures the more tolerable will disappointments be. Abel he takes for vanity, given by a mother so taken up with her first possession that another son was as nothing to her, and he presses the name on the whole race, since every man at his best estate is vanity. Ellicott looks ahead to what the chapter will show, the founding of a family godless and wanton which nevertheless far outstripped the sons of Seth in the arts of civilisation, adding tillage and pasture to metallurgy and music.
2:
The Hebrew says only that she added to bear, and the interpreters make what they can of it. Gill allows that the second birth may have followed the next year, though some have thought from the silence about a second conception that the two were born together; he passes on the common Jewish opinion that a twin sister was born with Abel, whom the Arabic writers call Lebuda. Clarke thinks the wording settles the matter for twins, since where successive births are recorded Scripture usually mentions conceiving and bringing forth for each child, whereas here it is simply that she added to bring forth Abel his brother. Ellicott looks instead at the interval before Seth, since Adam was a hundred and thirty when that son was born, which leaves a long period for the family to increase and for the characters of these two to develop; in the one he sees a rough strong nature that took the hard work as it found it and subdued the ground with muscular energy, in the other a nature more refined and thoughtful.

On the name they agree in sense and differ about its occasion. Gill notes that it means not mourning, as Josephus said, but vanity, either because Eve made no such account of this son as of her first, or because by a spirit of prophecy she foresaw that he should be deprived of life in a violent manner. Keil hears in it that her joy was soon overcome by the discovery of the vanity of this earthly life, the word meaning nothingness, whether it marked a feeling of sorrow at the child's weakness or was a presentiment of his untimely death. Ellicott dismisses Oppert's Assyrian etymology, since the Hebrew Hebel means a thing unstable and not abiding, like a breath or vapour, and doubts that a mother named her child from a presentiment at all; more probably the title was given after his death, when his sorrowing relatives called him the Breath that had passed away, naming in infancy being a later custom. Calvin will not have the name spoken in contempt, as if the child were superfluous, which he calls perfectly absurd; rather Eve, having celebrated in her firstborn the joy that suddenly burst upon her, turned in her second to the recollection of the miseries of the human race, and wished a monument of her sorrow to stand in his name, holding up a common mirror to admonish her whole progeny.

The two callings are read as honourable and as significant. Keil observes that the occupations are noticed on account of what follows, that Adam had no doubt begun both, and that God himself had pointed out each to him, tillage in the employment assigned in Eden and the keeping of cattle in the clothing he gave; nor can agriculture ever be entirely separated from the rearing of cattle, since a man requires clothing as well as food. Clarke counts three primitive employments, Adam a gardener, Abel a shepherd, Cain a farmer, and calls them the most rational and the best calculated to prevent strife and an immoderate love of the world. Calvin insists that both lives were in themselves holy and laudable, the cultivation of the earth being commanded by God and the feeding of sheep no less honourable, so that the whole of rustic life was innocent and simple; whence he infers that the brothers had been well instructed by their father, a thing the rite of sacrifice confirms. Cain's life, he adds, was in appearance very well regulated, since he cultivated the duties of piety and sought a maintenance by honest labour, as became a provident and sober father of a family. Wesley finds an advantage in the other calling, since a pastoral life most befriends contemplation and devotion, Moses and David having kept sheep and in their solitudes conversed with God.
3:
The phrase rendered in process of time is literally at the end of days, and the question is what period is meant. Gill reports the view that it means the end of a week, on the seventh day, but objects that this proceeds on a hypothesis not sufficiently established, that a sabbath was already appointed to be kept religiously; he prefers Aben Ezra's reading, at the end of the year, which would fall after harvest, when the fruits of the earth were gathered in and gratitude was in season, as the Israelites afterwards had their feast of ingathering. He adds that the Targum of Jonathan fixes the day to the fourteenth of Nisan, as though it were the passover, a feast instituted two thousand years later. Clarke inclines the other way, mentioning the anniversary of the creation but thinking the sabbath more probable, since divine worship was certainly instituted in that family. Wesley leaves both open and settles for some set time, and Henry does the same, allowing the end of the year, or an annual fast in remembrance of the fall, or the seventh day.

What was brought, and to whom, is described more confidently. Henry has the brothers bring their offerings to Adam as the priest of the family, and thinks there was a divine appointment given to Adam for it, as a token of God's favour and of his thoughts of love towards him and his, notwithstanding their apostasy; by it God would try Adam's faith in the promise and his obedience to the remedial law, settle a correspondence again between heaven and earth, and give shadows of good things to come. Clarke describes the worship as very simple in its original institution and consisting of two parts, thanksgiving to God as the author and dispenser of all the bounties of nature, with oblations indicative of that gratitude, and piacular sacrifices to his justice and holiness, implying a conviction of sinfulness, confession of transgression, and faith in the promised Deliverer. Of Cain's own offering he notes that the word is the one explained in Leviticus as an offering of fine flour with oil and frankincense, in general a gratitude offering, by which he testified his belief in God as Lord of the universe and dispenser of secular blessings.

Henry draws the lessons out at length. The first is the antiquity of the thing itself, since the religious worship of God is no novel invention but an ancient institution, that which was from the beginning, the good old way; truth got the start of error, and piety of profaneness. The second concerns children, since it is a good thing for them to be well taught when they are young and trained up betimes in religious services, that when they come to be capable of acting for themselves they may of their own accord bring an offering to God. The third concerns the measure of the gift, since we should every one of us honour God with what we have, according as he has prospered us; their offerings answered to their employments and possessions, and our merchandise and our hire, whatever they are, must be holiness to the Lord. The last is a warning, that hypocrites and evil doers may be found going as far as the best of God's people in the external services of religion. Cain brought an offering with Abel, and Cain's is mentioned first, as if he were the more forward of the two; a hypocrite may hear as many sermons, say as many prayers and give as much alms as a good Christian, and yet for want of sincerity come short of acceptance, as the Pharisee and the publican both went up to the temple to pray.
4:
What Abel brought is examined closely. Gill takes the firstlings as a type of Christ, Jehovah's firstborn, the Lamb of God that takes away the sin of the world, without spot or blemish, and fitly signified by a lamb for his innocence, harmlessness and meekness. Clarke reports Kennicott's reading, that the words mean Abel brought it also, a gratitude offering like his brother's, and besides this brought of the first-born of his flock, by which alone he acknowledged himself a sinner; on that view Hebrews calls his sacrifice not a more excellent but a greater one, and the testimony borne to his gifts in the plural shows he brought more than one. On that reading Cain, whom Clarke calls the father of Deism, brought a thank-offering to the God of the universe without acknowledging any need of a vicarious sacrifice. He adds that Magee has criticised the distinction, showing that the word for the unbloody offering is used of both kinds, but thinks little is gained by the counter-criticism. Jamieson, Fausset and Brown look instead at the verb of acceptance, which signifies to look at a thing with a keen earnest glance and has been rendered to kindle into a fire, so that the divine approval of Abel's offering was shown in its being consumed.

Why one was accepted and not the other is answered from the offerer rather than the gift. Calvin notes the order Moses observes, since he does not say the oblation pleased God but begins with the person, signifying that God regards no works whose doer is not already accepted; man sees what is apparent, but God looks into the heart, and if a man polluted in soul contaminates by his touch things otherwise clean, how can what proceeds from himself be pure? Even the heathen poets require a clean heart and pure hands, whence the rite of washing before sacrifice among all nations. Gill denies that the matter of Cain's offering was the difficulty, and puts it down to its being brought in a formal and hypocritical manner, without regard to the Messiah and his sacrifice. Wesley sets out three differences: in the characters of the persons; in the offerings, since Cain's was only a sacrifice of acknowledgment while Abel's was one of atonement whose blood was shed in order to remission; and greatest of all, that Abel offered in faith, with an eye to God's will and in dependence on the promise of a Redeemer.

How Cain learned of the difference is disputed. Calvin will not have the Hebrews' account, that the sacrifice was consumed by celestial fire, since we ought not to invent miracles for which we have no testimony of Scripture; he thinks Cain judged rather from what followed, seeing it went better with his brother and inferring that God was pleased with the one and displeased with the other, for to hypocrites nothing seems of greater value than earthly blessing. He also dismisses the Jewish notion that Cain defrauded God with barren or half-filled ears, since the evil lay deeper, in impurity of heart. On the anger itself they agree. Ellicott renders the Hebrew as it burned to Cain exceedingly, his heart being full of hot indignant feelings at the preference shown to a younger brother; Wesley finds in the fallen countenance not so much grief as malice and rage, betrayed by a sullen churlish down-look; and Clarke observes that the displeasure which should have been turned against his own unhumbled heart was turned against an innocent brother. Calvin sees in him the likeness of every wicked man who wishes to be esteemed just, labouring at external works while presenting God with a mask, and who, when the labour gains him nothing, complains and then rages, so that if he were able he would tear God from his throne; being unable, he pours his fury on his brother instead.
6:
The question is read as mercy rather than enquiry. Gill says it was not asked in ignorance of Cain's wrath but to bring him to a conviction of the sins which had caused his sacrifice to be rejected, and so to repentance and amendment, and to show him that he had no cause to be displeased with God or with his brother, the fault lying in himself. Clarke calls it a gracious warning and a preventive of the meditated crime. Henry makes it an instance of God's patience and condescending goodness that he should deal thus tenderly with so bad a man in so bad an affair, being not willing that any should perish but that all should come to repentance, and he sets the scene beside two others, the father of the prodigal arguing the case with his elder son, and God reasoning with the Israelites who said that his way was not equal.

Henry takes the form of the question as a lesson in self-examination. God puts Cain himself upon enquiring into the cause of his discontent and considering whether it were indeed a just cause; and two things follow from that. The first is that God takes notice of all our sinful passions and discontents, since there is not an angry look, an envious look, nor a fretful look that escapes his observing eye. The second is that most of our sinful heats and disquietudes would soon vanish before a strict and impartial enquiry into their cause. Why am I wroth? Is there a real cause, a just cause, a proportionable cause for it? Why am I so soon angry, why so very angry, and so implacable? He adds that Cain had no reason to be angry with God, who had proceeded according to the settled and invariable rules of a government suited to a state of probation, setting before men life and death, the blessing and the curse, and rendering to them according to their works, so that they are differenced only as they difference themselves.

Calvin is more interested in how the words came. He takes the address as a citation to God's tribunal, that the wretched man might understand his rage could profit him nothing: he wished honour for his sacrifices, and because he did not obtain it he was furiously angry, without considering that it was through his own fault he had failed of his wish, and that had he been conscious of his inward evil he would have ceased to expostulate with God and to rage against a guiltless brother. On the manner of the speaking Moses says nothing, whether a vision was presented, or an oracle heard from heaven, or a secret inspiration given; but Calvin rejects the suggestion that Adam spoke as the prophet and interpreter of God in censuring his son, calling it constrained and even frigid. He understands what good men intend by such a fancy, namely to honour the external ministry of the word and to cut off the occasion Satan takes to insinuate his illusions under colour of revelation, and grants that nothing is more useful than that pious minds should be kept under the order of preaching rather than seeking the mind of God in erratic speculations. Yet the word was delivered from the beginning by oracles, so that afterwards, when administered by the hands of men, it might receive the greater reverence; and though the office of teaching was enjoined upon Adam, they who think God spoke only through his ministers too violently restrict the words of Moses, and greatly abate the force of the divine reprimand.
7:
Ellicott calls this the most difficult verse of the chapter, capable of a satisfactory sense if we refuse to read the ideas of a later age into so ancient a narrative. Literally it asks, if thou doest well, is there not lifting up; and since the fallen countenance has just been mentioned and lifting up is often applied to the countenance, the promise is that instead of a downcast look Cain shall lift up his head and have peace beaming in his eyes from a quiet conscience. Calvin surveys the older attempts and rejects most: the Greek translators, working before the vowel points, struck into an extraneous sense, while among those who keep the Hebrew some refer the word to Cain's countenance, some to the remission of sins, and some to honour. His own reading is that it means acceptance, opposed to rejection, and refers to the sacrifices: God was ready to receive them with outstretched hands if they ceased to be faulty. Gill allows a general and a particular sense, either doing good works in a right manner, whence the saying that not nouns but adverbs make good works, or offering rightly, in the faith of the promised seed.

The clause about sin at the door divides them. Clarke takes the noun in a sense he says he has traced through more than a hundred places of the Old Testament, a sin-offering, so that an animal proper for atonement is now couching at the door of Cain's fold; his fault had been to bring none when his brother brought one, and God graciously tells him his case is not yet desperate. How many sinners perish, Clarke adds, not because there is no Saviour able and willing, but because they will not use what is within their power. Ellicott gives two constructions and prefers the second. On the first, sin crouches like a beast of prey at the door and its desire is to make Cain its victim, though he shall rule over it; the fatal objection is that sin is feminine while the verb and pronouns are masculine, which most Jewish interpreters override with what he calls a feeble explanation. On the second, sin crouches near and Cain must stand on his guard, the desire and the rule belonging to his brother. Wesley keeps the shortest sense: sin only hinders his acceptance.

The last clause most of them refer to the birthright rather than to sin. Clarke says expressly that these words are not spoken of sin, as many have understood, but of Abel's submission to Cain as his superior, to remove Cain's envy. Wesley says the same, that Abel shall continue to respect him as an elder brother, God's acceptance of the younger man's offering not transferring the birthright Cain was jealous of. Ellicott fills in the circumstances: Abel was outstripping him in wealth, his flocks multiplying and perhaps the younger brothers attaching themselves to him. He reads the remonstrance as evidence of a struggle in Cain's conscience, since Jehovah would not have reasoned thus kindly with a man altogether reprobate, and calls it a gratuitous assumption that the murder followed immediately on the sacrifice. Calvin puts the reproof more sharply: the blame of the whole evil lay with Cain, whose complaint was foolish since he had taken no care to amend the defects of his offering, and who did what wicked men do when convicted, trying vainly to transfer the cause of the evil to others. Wesley draws out two senses, either that Cain would have been accepted had he done well, since there is not a damned sinner in hell but, had he done well, had been a glorified saint in heaven, or that he might yet be accepted if he would repent and bring his sacrifice better, which shows how early the gospel was preached and offered to one of the chief of sinners.
8:
The verse has a hole in it, and they differ about how to fill it. Clarke notes that the Hebrew says only that Cain said to his brother, the best editions leaving a space with a mark referring to a note that something is wanting; the deficiency is supplied by the Samaritan text, the Syriac, the Vulgate, the Septuagint, the Targums and the Coptic, all reading, let us go out into the field. Since the words are lost from every known manuscript and yet stood in copies used before the Christian era, he thinks they may safely be counted part of the sacred text. Ellicott is more cautious: no Hebrew authority but the Jerusalem Targum supports the addition, though the versions carry great weight, the Hebrew manuscripts being all comparatively modern and representing only the Masoretic recension. He rules out our version's rendering, which would imply that Cain had triumphed for a time over his anger and resumed friendly intercourse, and concludes that either we accept the versions or must regard the passage as beyond our powers. Gill and Clarke both pass on the Jerusalem Targum's report of their talk, Cain arguing that there is no judgment and no Judge and no mercy in the world's creation or government, and Abel answering point by point.

How the quarrel became murder is variously imagined. Clarke supposes the first murder was the fruit of a religious dispute, and remarks that millions have since been sacrificed to bigotry and intolerance; here originated the many-headed monster of religious persecution, every persecutor being a son of the old murderer. Ellicott will not have it premeditated, since Cain did not know what a human death was, and offers Philippson's suggestion of the perpetual struggle between husbandmen holding fixed plots and shepherds whose flocks stray on tilled ground: perhaps Abel's flocks had trespassed, and Cain, going to remonstrate, had his envy stirred at his brother's affluence, until in a fit of anger he tried to enforce his mastery by blows, and before he well knew what he was doing stood in terror before the first human corpse. Calvin weighs two accounts of the talking: either Cain dissembled and spoke familiarly to keep up an appearance of fraternal concord until the opportunity came, whence the rule that hypocrites are most to be dreaded when they converse under the pretext of friendship, or, as he rather inclines to think, he broke out in open accusation against his brother.

Henry sets down the aggravations. It was his own brother, whom he ought to have loved, and a younger brother, whom he ought to have protected; a good brother, who had never provoked him in word or deed; he had fair warning and persisted; he covered the design with a show of friendship, as Joab kissed Abner and Absalom feasted Amnon; and in killing him he struck directly at God, since God's accepting Abel was the provocation pretended, and he hated Abel for the very reason that God loved him. The murder was the more inhuman, Henry adds, because there were then so few men in the world. He traces the root as well: Adam's eating of forbidden fruit seemed but a little sin and opened the door to the greatest, and as Abel leads the van in the noble army of martyrs, so Cain stands in front of the ignoble army of persecutors; rash anger is heart-murder, and he that hates his brother wants only an opportunity. Clarke marks what was new: this is Satan's first triumph, not merely a death but a violent one, not of an ordinary person but of the most holy man then living, and by a brother's hand. Wesley turns to the other side: the first who dies is a saint, and the first to the grave went to heaven, God securing the first-fruits of those that first opened the womb into another world.
9:
Gill supposes the question came when Cain next appeared to offer without his brother, asked not from ignorance but to bring him to conviction and confession, the mention of the relation being itself an aggravation. Henry sets it as a trial, since civil courts were not yet erected and God himself sits Judge, being the God to whom vengeance belongs; some think Cain was examined on the next sabbath, when the sons of God came to present themselves before the Lord and Abel was missing, whose place did not use to be empty, for the God of heaven takes notice who is present at and who is absent from public ordinances. Cain is asked, Henry adds, not merely because there was cause to suspect him but because God knew him guilty, the question being put to draw a confession, since those who would be justified before God must accuse themselves.

The answer is read as a second crime. Keil states the rule shortly: defiance grows with sin and punishment keeps pace with guilt: Adam and Eve feared before God and acknowledged their sin, while Cain boldly denies his. Henry finds him covering a deliberate murder with a deliberate lie, so that in Cain the devil was both murderer and liar from the beginning; those are strangely blind who think it possible to conceal their sins from a God who sees all, and strangely hard who think it desirable to conceal them from a God who pardons only those that confess. On the retort Henry is sharper still, since Cain charges his Judge with folly and injustice when he should have said, Am not I my brother's murderer? Wesley gives the impudence plainly, that surely he is old enough to take care of himself, and adds the reflection some have heard in it upon providence, Art not thou his keeper? Calvin notes the cavil more exactly: Cain thinks to escape by pleading he had no express command to take care of his brother, and so owed no account of him.

Whose voice put the question is Calvin's concern. Those who suppose the father made the inquiry enervate the whole instruction, since God cited the murderer to his tribunal as if he had thundered from heaven; and though he may have been interrogated by the silent examinations of conscience, it was by a divine voice and not by the voice of a man. From this Calvin draws his chief lesson: as often as the secret compunctions of conscience invite us to reflect upon our sins we should remember that God himself is speaking with us, that interior sense being his peculiar judgement-seat, where he exercises his jurisdiction. Let those whose consciences accuse them beware, therefore, lest after Cain's example they confirm themselves in obstinacy, which is truly to kick against God; prodigious was the stupor of the man who ferociously rejected the reproof of a God from whose hand he could not escape; and it happens daily, the human heart being so entangled in winding labyrinths that the wicked easily add contempt of God to their crimes, though secretly burned as with a hot iron all the while. Ellicott reconstructs the state of mind instead. Cain went away at first scarcely conscious of the greatness of his crime, having asserted his rights against a younger son's usurpation of his privileges, so that if he used force it was his brother's fault for resisting; but he could not quiet his conscience, remorse tracked his footsteps, and when Abel came not to the household and the question was asked, the voice of God repeated it in his own heart. Henry ends on the duty the retort denies: a charitable concern for our brethren as their keepers is strictly required and generally neglected, and those who take no care to prevent hurt to them in body, goods or good name speak Cain's language.
10:
Wesley describes the figure: the words speak as if the blood were both witness and prosecutor, God's knowledge testifying against Cain and God's justice demanding satisfaction, while the earth did as it were blush to see her face stained with such blood, and opened her mouth to hide what she could not hinder. Clarke supposes Cain had buried the body to prevent the murder from being known, which is what the opening of the ground implies; he mentions also the opinion that the cry is that of Abel's widow and children, his occupation and sacrifices making it probable he was a father of a family, though probability is all we can expect here. Keil quotes Delitzsch, that innocent blood has no voice discernible by human ears but has one that reaches God, as the cry of a wicked deed demanding vengeance, murder being one of the sins that cry to heaven. Ellicott follows the thought forward: with the first shedding of human blood there sprang up the ominous conviction that the earth will grant no peace to the wretch who has stained her fair face with the life stream of man; but the blood of Jesus speaks better things than Abel's, the one voice crying for justice and retribution, the other for reconciliation and peace.

Calvin reads it as a court scene brought to its end. God no longer asks whether the thing was done, but pronounces in a single word that Cain was the doer, and so aggravates the atrocity. Advocates, he observes, place their first defence in denying the fact, and where it cannot be denied have recourse to qualifying circumstances; Cain is driven from both, and we are warned that pretexts are heaped together in vain when sinners are cited to God's tribunal. Three things Calvin finds shown: that God is cognizant of men's deeds though none accuse them; that he holds the life of man too dear to let innocent blood be shed with impunity; and that he cares for the pious after death as well as before. Abel was speechless when his throat was being cut, yet after death the voice of his blood was more vehement than any eloquence of an orator; which Calvin calls a wonderfully sweet consolation to good men unjustly harassed, since the placid silence of the soul raises cries that fill heaven and earth.

The curse is read out of the ground. Gill takes it that Cain is cut off from the benefit of the earth and from any settled dwelling in it. Keil weighs two constructions of the preposition, either away from the earth, so that it afford him no quiet resting-place, or out of the earth, by its withdrawing its strength, and inclines to the second: compelled to drink innocent blood, the earth rebels against the murderer and yields no produce when he tills it, as Canaan is said to have spued out its inhabitants. He rejects as unsupported the notion that the soil became an accomplice by drinking the blood. Calvin rejects the same notion in another form, since some imagine cruelty ascribed to the earth, as though it were a wild beast that had drunk the blood; rather clemency is imputed to it, since in abhorrence of the pollution it opened its mouth to cover what a brother's hand had shed, there being more humanity in the earth than in the man. Nor need we imagine a miracle of unusual opening; judgment was committed to the earth so that Cain might understand his judge need not be summoned from a distance, no angel descending from heaven when the earth offered itself as avenger. Wesley says the same: God could have taken vengeance by a stroke from heaven, but chose to continue him upon the earth and make even that his curse, the ground that fell to his share being made unfruitful by the blood of Abel.
12:
Calvin treats the first clause as expounding the curse just pronounced, since it says more clearly that the ground defrauds its cultivator of the fruit of his toil. To the objection that this was already laid on all men in Adam he answers that something of the blessing hitherto remaining was now further withdrawn from the murderer, that he might feel the very earth hostile to him, God designing in the first murder a singular example of malediction to be remembered in all ages. Gill notes that tillage was the business Cain had been brought up in. On the wandering Calvin sets aside the distinction some draw between the two Hebrew words, and says the sense is that wherever Cain came he should be as robbers are, who have no quiet resting-place, the face of every man striking terror into them while they have a horror of solitude besides. He meets a second objection, that to be a stranger on the earth is rather the condition of the sons of God, by observing that the faithful carry a sedate mind wherever necessity drives them, whereas Cain was condemned to find no region where his mind would not be restless, and even the first builder of a city was always restless in his own nest.

What Cain cried next is disputed in translation. Clarke prefers the margin, that the words may be rendered, Is my crime too great to be forgiven, since the noun signifies the crime rather than the punishment and the verb means to remit; they were uttered, he thinks, on the verge of black despair. Henry weighs both readings. If the words are those of despair they affront the mercy of God, since there is forgiveness with the God of pardons for the greatest sinners, though those forfeit it who despair of it; just now Cain made nothing of his sin, and now he is in the other extreme, Satan driving his vassals from presumption to despair, and we cannot think too ill of sin provided we do not think it unpardonable. But Henry judges the language rather that of indignation, complaining not of the greatness of the sin but of the extremity of the punishment, so that instead of justifying God Cain condemns him. Calvin reaches the same conclusion by another road. Nearly all commentators call it desperation, and it is true that the reprobate are never conscious of their evils till an inescapable ruin overtakes them, as Judas confessed his sin yet fled from God's presence; but Calvin takes the words in their proper signification, that a greater punishment is imposed on him than he can bear, so that Cain complains of the severity of his judgment, as devils do who feel themselves justly tormented and still charge God with cruelty.

Henry follows the complaint into parts. Cain sees himself excluded from the favour of his God, being cursed and hidden from God's face, which is the true nature of the curse, those being cursed indeed who are for ever shut out from God's love and care. He sees himself expelled from the comforts of this life, since as good have no place on earth as not have a settled place. And he sees himself exposed to the ill-will of all mankind, so that wherever he wanders he goes in peril of his life, or thinks so, and like a man in debt thinks every one he meets a bailiff; unpardoned guilt fills men with continual terrors, and it is better to fear and not sin than to sin and fear. Henry adds Lightfoot's suggestion that the last words are a wish, that any who find him may kill him, since being bitter in soul he longs for death and it comes not. Keil observes the answer: though Cain expressed no penitence but only fear of punishment, God displayed his long-suffering and gave a promise.
14:
Gill explains the banishment as exclusion not from the earth but from a quiet settlement in it, from society and converse with its inhabitants, and especially from the ground he had manured and the place where his parents dwelt; to be sent into a strange uninhabited country was a sore punishment. Clarke counts the parts and finds Cain adding to them. God had named two, the cursed ground and the vagabond life; to these the man adds being hidden from God's face, which Clarke takes as expulsion from the place near Paradise where God manifested his presence and the first parents resorted as to an oracle; the apprehension of being slain, since all men then were of one family and each had a right to avenge a kinsman; and the terrors of a guilty conscience, to which he thinks Paul alludes in speaking of destruction from the Lord's presence. Calvin allows that Cain reasons justly, since the hand of God alone preserves us amid so many dangers, and they spoke prudently who said our life hangs by a thread; yet he notes what the fear reveals, that since man is a social animal it is a portentous thing that the meeting of any man should be formidable to the murderer.

The answer turns on a single particle. Gill reports the rendering of it as two words meaning not so, denying both Cain's fear and his wish to be killed by the first man he met, and prefers verily or surely; God's will was that Cain should not die at once but live a long miserable life, for a terror to others. Ellicott notes that most versions have not so, which requires only a slight change of the text, and explains the sentence given instead: the punishment was severe because the crime sprang from violent passions, but the life was not taken because the act was not premeditated, murder being more than Cain had meant, while anyone killing him would be a murderer indeed, so the vengeance would be sevenfold, that is complete, seven being the number of perfection. In this, he adds, is the germ of the law that set apart cities of refuge for the involuntary manslayer. Calvin rejects the Jewish reading which breaks the sentence in two and refers the sevenfold punishment to Cain himself; the clause runs on continuously, and God grants nothing to the murderer for his own sake but consults for posterity, the order of nature having been awfully violated. Wesley puts the reason shortly: God having said vengeance is his, it had been a daring usurpation for any man to take the sword out of his hand.

On the sign they divide between exegesis and curiosity. Ellicott says the common rendering suggests an utterly false idea, since Cain was not branded in any way; the Hebrew says Jehovah appointed unto him a sign that no one finding him should slay him, probably some natural phenomenon whose regular recurrence would assure him of his security. Clarke gathers from Shuckford the conjectures made and calls them frivolously curious: that Cain was made paralytic, from the Septuagint's groaning and trembling; that it was a letter of the divine name; that it was Abel's dog, which constantly accompanied him; and, from one rabbi wiser than all the rest, a long horn growing out of his forehead. With Shuckford he would translate that the Lord appointed to Cain a token, since to have marked him would have been the likeliest way to bring on him all the evils he dreaded. Wesley dismisses the question in a line: God has not told us what the mark was, and therefore the conjectures of men are vain. Calvin asks only what it was for: it was set to strike terror into all, who might see in it as in a mirror the tremendous judgment of God against bloody men.
16:
Gill offers two senses of the departure, either from the place where the Lord had been speaking with him, or from where the divine Majesty usually resided at the east of Eden, Cain being now forbidden to appear among God's worshippers; and he notes a place near Tripoli in Syria, mentioned by Polybius and Strabo as the face of God, which may have been so named from a tradition that there God's presence was enjoyed after the expulsion from Eden. Henry reads the going out as a willing surrender of that part of the sentence: Cain renounced religion and was content to forego its privileges so that he might not be under its precepts, forsaking Adam's family and altar and never coming among good people again. Hypocritical professors who have trifled with God, he adds, are justly left to themselves, and hell itself is destruction from the presence of the Lord, a perpetual banishment from the fountain of all good. Ellicott supposes Adam's family worshipped with their faces towards Paradise, so that Cain, migrating from the whole land of Eden, reckoned himself beyond the range of the vision of God. Calvin allows two accounts, either that Cain, having lived in the earth as in an abode belonging to God, now wanders like an exile beyond the limits of his protection, or that he had stood at the bar until condemned and, the speaking over, hastened elsewhere to escape the eyes of God.

The land takes its character from its name. Keil says the situation cannot be determined, and that Nod denotes a land of flight and banishment set against Eden, the land of delight, where Jehovah walked with men. Calvin thinks the region was named from its inhabitant, and infers from its lying to the east of Paradise that the garden itself must have been a limited place, since only a bounded spot can have one region opposite it. Clarke reports that since the word is the same as that for a vagabond, some would render the clause as saying that Cain went out from the presence of the Lord, from the east of Eden, and dwelt a vagabond on the earth, so that the curse was thereby accomplished. Henry and Wesley take the name as descriptive of the man rather than the ground, since the land he dwelt in was to him a land of shaking or trembling, because of the continual restlessness of his own spirit; those who depart from God, Wesley adds, cannot find rest anywhere else, and after Cain went out from the presence of the Lord he never rested.

Where he went, and with whom, is guessed at more freely. Ellicott records that Knobel supposed the land to be China, which he thinks too remote, and that read without vowels the word becomes India; all that is certain is that Cain emigrated into Eastern Asia, and since none of Noah's descendants in the table of nations are described as travelling eastward, many follow Philippson and Knobel in regarding the Mongol race as his offspring. Keil is concerned with the wife instead, since the text assumes as self-evident that she went with him into exile and that she was a daughter of Adam and so her husband's sister; the marriage of brothers and sisters was inevitable among the children of the first men if the human race was actually to descend from a single pair, and may be justified against the later Mosaic prohibition, since the sons and daughters of Adam represented not merely the family but the genus. Henry finds defiance in the choice of ground, since it was on the east of Eden that the cherubim stood with the flaming sword, and there Cain chose his lot as if to defy the terrors of the Lord, distinguishing his accursed generation from the holy seed.
17:
Who the wife was the text does not say, and Gill will not decide whether she was his sister or a niece by another son of Adam, this being about the hundred and thirtieth year; at first, he grants, Cain could marry none but a sister. He passes on two rival traditions: the Jews say Cain's own twin sister was not beautiful, so that he said he would kill his brother and take his wife, while the Arabic writers say Adam would have had each brother marry the other's twin sister, and Cain refused because his own was the handsomer. Ellicott reasons from the promise that Eve's conception should be greatly multiplied, so that a numerous offspring had grown up before Seth, only the eldest sons being named in the genealogies; one of Adam's daughters apparently clave to her brother in spite of the sentence of banishment and followed him as his wife. Calvin infers from the silence that Cain had married before the murder, since it would have been worth recording that a sister could be found who would not shrink from a man defiled with a brother's blood, and would choose exile over her father's house; and he calls it a prodigy that a man who imagined he had as many enemies as there were men should raise children instead of hiding in some remote solitude.

The name of the son is read as a sign of some change in him. Clarke observes that it signifies instructed or dedicated, especially in sacred things, and takes it for some proof of Cain's repentance that he dedicated this son to God, to minister in his father's stead in the office from which Cain was excluded. Ellicott gives the same word two senses, to train and to dedicate, and notes that in old times the ideas were closely allied, since teaching generally took the form of initiation into sacred rites; so whoever gave the name, it purposed that the child should be trained and consecrated, and Cain must by now have put off the habits which led him into so terrible a crime. This, he adds, prepares us for the Cainites' rapid advance in the arts of civilisation.

The city divides them more sharply. Calvin finds it at first sight contrary to the sentence, since Adam and the rest passed their lives in hovels or under the open heaven while the exile builds a city; he concludes that the man, oppressed by conscience and not thinking himself safe within his own walls, contrived a new kind of defence, the others living dispersed through the fields only because they were less afraid. Yet pride was mixed with the fear, since he called the city after his son, when he ought rather to have chosen that his name be buried for ever, his memory passing on only to be held in execration. To those who ask where Cain found architects and citizens, Calvin answers by asking what authority they have for supposing the city was of squared stone and built at much expense, since nothing more can be gathered than that he surrounded himself with walls of the rudest materials. Ellicott reads the verb as an imperfect, that Cain began to build, there being not yet population enough for a city, and sees in the design a wise ruler rather than a religious man, whose purpose was much what the builders of Babel had, to keep mankind together in one powerful community. Wesley takes the building as a token of settled separation from the church of God, and says the names that follow are but just mentioned, as not valued in comparison with God's children. Gill notes that of Irad nothing further is recorded in sacred or profane history, and Ellicott, that the city probably suggested his name, these names having been so corrupted by transcribers that certainty is not to be had.
19:
Lamech is remembered first for a bad innovation. Gill calls him the first we read of who introduced polygamy, against the institution by which one man and one woman were to become one flesh, and notes that the practice, begun in the race of wicked Cain, was afterwards followed by some among the people of God and connived at for the hardness of their hearts; he reports and rejects Jarchi's account that before the flood men kept one wife for children and another for pleasure, since both of Lamech's wives bore sons. Clarke says he was the first who dared to reverse the order of God, and that from him polygamy has been retained and defended to the present day. Calvin thinks it of little consequence whether he was impelled by desire of enlarging his family or by mere lust, since either way he corrupted nature's laws with brutal contempt of God; and finds a providence in the choice of the first offender, the Lord willing that the corruption of marriage should proceed from the house of Cain, that polygamists might be ashamed of the example. Henry draws two warnings: that those who desert God's ordinances lay themselves open to all manner of temptation, and that when a bad custom is begun by bad men, better men are sometimes drawn in unwarily, as Jacob and David were afterwards ensnared in this very sin.

The sons are remembered for better things. Henry counts three, a famous shepherd whom the shepherds of that age and after called father, a musician who first gave rules for that noble art, and a smith who improved the working of brass and iron for war and husbandry; when Jabal had set them in a way to be rich, Jubal put them in a way to be merry, and he matches the three against the heathen gods, Jabal their Pan, Jubal their Apollo, Tubal-cain their Vulcan. Clarke fills in the inventions: tent-making and the management of cattle in the first, stringed and wind instruments in the second, both words being generic, and in the third the first smith on record. Some of these arts were useless while man was upright but became necessary after the fall, and as the power to get wealth is from God so is the invention of useful arts.

Calvin makes that his chief point. With the evils that proceeded from the family of Cain some good had been blended, since the invention of arts serving the common use of life is a gift of God not to be despised; and it is wonderful that the race which fell most deeply should have excelled the rest of Adam's posterity in rare endowments. The sons of Cain, though deprived of the Spirit of regeneration, were endued with gifts of no despicable kind, the rays of divine light having shone widely on unbelieving nations, and the liberal arts have descended to us from the heathen; God enriched them so that their impiety might have less excuse, but we are to value far more the grace of regeneration. Of music he says that though the harp ministers to pleasure rather than necessity it is not superfluous nor to be condemned, since it can serve the offices of religion if free from vicious attractions and from the foolish delight which seduces men from better employments. Henry allows the same and turns it: common gifts are given to bad men while God chooses the foolish things of the world, and here was a father of shepherds and of musicians but not a father of the faithful, one to teach in brass and iron but none to teach the knowledge of the Lord. On the last of the three, Gill notes that many identify him with Vulcan, the names and the trade agreeing, and Wesley thinks the heathen god came from him; why the sister is named neither says.
23:
Clarke observes that the speech stands in hemistichs in the original, and since nothing of the kind occurs earlier thinks it very probably the oldest piece of poetry in the world. Wesley confesses at once that the passage is extremely obscure, since we know neither whom Lamech slew, nor on what occasion, nor what ground he had to be so confident of the divine protection. Calvin traces the obscurity to the abruptness of Moses, and clears away the Jewish fable that Lamech was a blind hunter whose boy misdirected his arrow so that it killed Cain in the woods, after which the master killed the boy; Clarke declines to trouble his readers with that tale, though Jerome followed it, and leaves the passage among those he calls inscrutable.

What the words claim is read three ways. Clarke supposes Lamech had slain a man in self-defence and that his wives feared the dead man's kindred would seek his life, so that he reasons with them: if the slayer of the wilful murderer Cain was threatened with sevenfold punishment, much more he who killed a man that had shed blood only in self-defence. He notes that the words may also be read interrogatively, Have I slain a man that I should be wounded, which makes a clearer sense but still supposes something said before. Calvin prefers to resolve the past tense into a future and take it indefinitely, so that Lamech is boasting he has strength enough to strike down any enemy whatever; the repetition of man and young man is Hebrew amplification and does not mean two persons, the sense being that let the mightiest come forward, there is none he will not dispatch. Gill allows a penitent and a boastful sense, either that Lamech is confessing what he has done and reckoning how much sorer a punishment he deserves than Cain, or that he is quieting his wives with an argument that none may safely touch him. Henry hears only the bravado: Lamech owns himself a man of a fierce and cruel disposition who would lay about him without mercy, and when his wives feared for his life answers in effect that he defies any man to set upon him.

The manner of the speech is as much noticed as its matter. Henry marks how haughtily and imperiously he addresses his wives, and observes that it is no marvel that a man who had broken one law of marriage by taking two wives should break another which bound him to be kind and tender to them; those are not always the most careful to do their own duty who are highest in their demands of respect from others. He notes too that it is a common thing for fierce and bloody men to glory in their shame, caring not how many lives are sacrificed to their resentments so long as they are feared. Calvin turns the same point on the wives, since the soothing arts of wives often mitigate cruel men, whereas Lamech cast the venom of his cruelty into their bosom and, so far from calming them, broke out in threats of indiscriminate slaughter like a furious wild beast. On the closing boast both are severe. Henry says he presumes impiously on God's protection, arguing that if God secured the life of Cain, who slew his brother upon no provocation, much more would he avenge one who killed only in a quarrel; and the reprieve of some sinners is thus abused to the hardening of others. Calvin says he perverts the declaration and mocks its severity, taking greater licence to sin as though God had granted murderers a singular privilege, not that he seriously believes it, but that, destitute of all sense of piety, he promises himself impunity and jestingly uses the name of God as an excuse, as Dionysius boasted that the gods favour the sacrilegious.
25:
Henry and Wesley notice that this is the first mention of Adam in the chapter, and that the murder of Abel and the apostasy of Cain were a very great grief to him and Eve, the more because their own wickedness now corrected them and their backslidings reproved them; their folly had given sin and death entrance into the world, and by it they were deprived of both their sons in one day. When parents are grieved by their children's wickedness, Henry adds, they should take occasion from it to lament that corruption of nature which was derived from them and is the root of bitterness. Calvin denies the inference that the first parents were left wholly childless, since it is incredible that while the benediction to increase and multiply was in its greatest force they should have been unfruitful through so many years; the house of Adam was already populous before Abel was slain, and Moses means only that the parents, horror-struck at the slaughter, abstained for a while from the conjugal bed. Gill notes that the Targum puts a hundred and thirty years between the murder and this birth, but Ussher, more probably, places Seth in the same year.

What Eve claimed for the child is variously grounded. Calvin says she means some peculiar seed, since others had been born before Abel's death, but the race being prone to evil nearly her whole family had corrupted itself, so that she had slight hope of the remaining multitude until God should raise up a new seed of which she might expect better things; she reckoned herself bereaved, in Abel, not of one son only but of her whole offspring. Clarke argues that she must have received some divine communication, since otherwise she could not have known that this son was appointed in Abel's place to continue the holy line by which the Messiah was to come; from which he concludes that the line was determined from the beginning and not first fixed in the days of Abraham. He traces it forward, since Seth's posterity alone continued after the flood, Noah being the tenth from Adam through him, and observes that wherever there were two or more sons the chosen one was pointed out by especial providence, Seth in Adam's family, Shem in Noah's, Isaac in Abraham's, so that when Christ came it might be seen that he came by promise and grace, and not by nature. Ellicott makes the same point of the succession, since instead of the third son simply taking the firstborn's place it is given to one specially marked out, probably by prophecy, as Solomon took the rights of primogeniture over Adonijah.

The name is read for its sense. Ellicott renders it appointed or substituted, the son being designated head of Adam's family. Henry gives it as set, settled or placed, because in his seed mankind should continue and from him the Messiah descend, and draws the contrast that while Cain, the head of the apostasy, is made a wanderer, Seth, from whom the true church was to come, is fixed, since in Christ and his church is the only true settlement. Henry finds in the birth a rule of God's dealing, that when he takes away one comfort he gives another instead, which may prove a greater blessing than the one in which they thought their lives were bound up; and he presses the point about the church, that the succession of confessors is the revival of the martyrs and as it were the resurrection of God's slain witnesses. Those who slay God's servants hope by that means to wear out the saints of the Most High, but they will be deceived, for God can out of stones raise up children to himself and make the blood of the martyrs the seed of the church, whose lands shall never be lost for want of heirs.
26:
The son's name is read from its root. Gill gives the usual interpretation, a weak, frail, mortal and miserable man, given by a father who observed the sorrows of life and the growing corruptions of the age; but he notes that it may also come from an Arabic word meaning to be sociable, man being sociable in religious as well as in civil things. Keil takes it from a verb meaning to be weak, so that the name expresses the knowledge of human frailty, the opposite of the pride displayed in the Cainite family, and observes that this feeling led to God and to the invocation which began under Enos. Ellicott doubts the derivation from mortality, for which there is no proof, and takes the word as the generic name for man, used so in Aramaic, where our Lord is styled the son of Enosh, the son of man and not the son of a mortal; in the words now in use for man he sees language itself growing.

What began is the harder question. Gill is careful that it does not mean the first calling upon God, since Adam and Abel and all good men had called on his name before. Wesley gives two senses. Either the worshippers of God began to stir themselves up to do more in religion than of late, worshipping now not only in closets and families but in public assemblies; or, as the margin reads, they began to be called by the name of the Lord, and so to distinguish themselves, since Cain and those who had deserted religion called themselves the sons of men, while those who adhered to God called themselves the sons of God. Calvin finds a synecdoche in the verb, calling upon God standing for his whole worship and named from its principal part, since God prefers this service of piety and faith to all sacrifices; and warns that Satan contrives nothing with greater care than to adulterate the pure invocation of God, so that the pomp of adoration is worth nothing unless this chief point be maintained. He takes the clause historically too, that the deluge of impiety was then so great that religion survived only with a few, until Seth begat a son like himself and had a rightly constituted family, whereupon the face of the Church began to appear. Ellicott makes the beginning belong to the name rather than the worship, the notion of divinity being now first attached to Jehovah, which Eve had used without any such thought.

A contrary reading has also been urged. Clarke reports that many eminent men would render the verb as began profanely, so that the words date idolatry's origin, most of the Jewish doctors being of that opinion; he sets out Maimonides. In the days of Enos, that account runs, the sons of Adam erred greatly, reasoning that since God had set the stars on high to govern the world it was meet that men should glorify what he honoured; whereupon they built temples to the stars and sacrificed to them, and false prophets stood up who claimed a command to worship them and made images, until the practice spread through all the world and the glorious and fearful name was forgotten out of the mouth of all living, save with a few, until Abraham was born. Calvin rejects the construction as a foolish figment, since Moses is not censuring superstitions here but commending the piety of one family which worshipped God in purity when religion elsewhere was polluted or extinct. Clarke draws the chapter's lesson from the other end: no uprightness of intention can atone for neglect of the positive commands of revelation, and he who brings a eucharistic offering while a sin-offering lies at the door copies Cain, whose envy had an evil eye merely because God was good, and begot hatred, and hatred malice, and malice murder.
